Getting started with zuint

Source: vignettes/zuint.Rmd
zuint.Rmd
library(zuint)

The four types

zuint has one type for each wide integer type that Arrow and DuckDB use. Each type gives up one bit pattern to NA, so its range is one value short of the full width.

zuint Arrow DuckDB Range
int64 int64 BIGINT ±(263 − 1)
uint64 uint64 UBIGINT 0 to 264 − 2
int128 arrow.opaque hugeint HUGEINT ±(2127 − 1)
uint128 arrow.opaque uhugeint UHUGEINT 0 to 2128 − 2

The constructors convert from numbers, strings and each other. A conversion is exact, or it gives NA with a warning:

uint64("18446744073709551614")
#> <uint64[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551614
int128("-0x7fff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff")
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] -170141183460469231731687303715884105727
int64(c(2^53, 1.5))
#> Warning in int64(c(2^53, 1.5)): 1 value could not be represented as int64 and
#> became NA.
#> <int64[2]>
#> [1] 9007199254740992               NA

int64 keeps the storage of bit64’s integer64 and has it as its second class, so packages that read integer64 read int64 unchanged.

Mixing types

When two types meet, the result is the smallest type that holds both, so no value is lost. int128 and uint128 hold different values, so they have no common type, and mixing them is an error.

zu_common_type(int64(1), uint64(1))
#> [1] "int128"
int64(-1) + uint64("18446744073709551614")
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551613
try(int128(1) + uint128(1))
#> Error in Ops.zu_int128(int128(1), uint128(1)) : 
#>   int128 and uint128 have no common type; convert one explicitly.

A double takes the zuint type if it is a whole number in range, and is an error otherwise; comparisons with doubles are exact and never an error:

int64(10) + 2
#> <int64[1]>
#> [1] 12
try(int64(10) + 0.5)
#> Error in Ops.zu_int64(int64(10), 0.5) : 
#>   A double must be integral and in range of int64 to mix with it. Convert it explicitly, or set options(zuint.double = "allow").
int64("9007199254740993") > 2^53
#> [1] TRUE

Overflow policies

The operators give NA with a warning when a result is out of range, as R’s integers do. The checked_*() functions make it an error, and the wrapping_*() functions compute modulo 264 or 2128:

big <- int64("9223372036854775807")
big + 1L
#> Warning in Ops.zu_int64(big, 1L): 1 result is out of range. NA produced.
#> <int64[1]>
#> [1] NA
try(checked_add(big, 1L))
#> Error in checked_add(big, 1L) : 1 result is out of range.
wrapping_mul(uint64("0xffffffff"), uint64("0xffffffff"))
#> <uint64[1]>
#> [1] 18446744065119617025

sum() keeps the type and is exact, or NA with a warning; mean() and median() are doubles computed from the exact values:

x <- int128(c("170141183460469231731687303715884105727", "1", "-1"))
sum(x)
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] 170141183460469231731687303715884105727
mean(int64(1:2))
#> [1] 1.5

Through engines and back

zu_duckdb_query() reads a query’s wide integer columns exactly, and zu_duckdb_register() hands a data frame back to DuckDB with their types:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
#> duckdb keeps downloaded extensions and secrets in a temporary directory:
#> ℹ /tmp/RtmpDmdVEF/duckdb
#> This is removed when the R session ends.
#> • Extensions are re-downloaded each session.
#> • Secrets are lost.
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = TRUE) (or create ~/.duckdb) to keep them (suitable for most users).
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to accept the temporary directory (and silence this message).
#> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives.
df <- zu_duckdb_query(con, "
  SELECT 18446744073709551614::UBIGINT AS id,
         -170141183460469231731687303715884105727::HUGEINT AS total
")
df
#>                     id                                    total
#> 1 18446744073709551614 -170141183460469231731687303715884105727
zu_duckdb_register(con, "back", df)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT typeof(id) AS id, typeof(total) AS total FROM back")
#>        id   total
#> 1 UBIGINT HUGEINT
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

The same columns go through Arrow tables, and so through Parquet files:

f <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(zu_arrow_table(df), f)
zu_from_arrow_table(arrow::read_parquet(f, as_data_frame = FALSE))
#>                     id                                    total
#> 1 18446744073709551614 -170141183460469231731687303715884105727

Underneath, zu_to_arrow() and zu_from_arrow() speak the Arrow C Data Interface directly, and nanoarrow::convert_array(array, int64()) uses them when nanoarrow is installed.

Where the class gets lost

Base functions that build their result from the bare values read the raw bits as numbers. The ones you meet first:

  • c(1L, x) and sum(2L, x) dispatch on their first argument, so with a base number first they never reach zuint: put the zuint vector first.
  • sapply(), unlist() and tapply() drop the class of what they collect: use zu_vapply(), or do.call(c, list).
  • ifelse() builds its answer from yes and no without their class.

zu_ifelse() and zu_vapply() keep the type:

x <- int64(c("-9223372036854775807", "5"))
zu_ifelse(x > 0L, x, int64(0))
#> <int64[2]>
#> [1] 0 5

For the same reason, serialize(ascii = TRUE) and dput() do not keep the values of negative int64 numbers or of NA; R’s default binary serialization does.
